title: Testing and debugging the agent
notes: A trace records every step of a run: the tool Scout chose, the input it sent and the result or error that came back.
To debug, reproduce the failing case, read the trace from the top and fix the first bad step; later mistakes often follow from it.
Most agent bugs are one of four: wrong tool, wrong arguments, an ignored tool error, or a loop.

slides.title: Testing and debugging the agent
slides.sub: Read the trace, find the first bad step, fix one thing
sentences: Scout will get things wrong. Every agent does.
What matters is how fast you can find out why.
In this lesson you learn to read a trace, and to spot the four bugs you'll meet most often.

slides.title: What is a trace?
slides.definition: A step-by-step record of one agent run: what Scout decided at each step, the input it sent, and what came back.

analogy.label: Think of it as
analogy.text: A flight recorder. When something goes wrong, you replay exactly what happened instead of guessing.

sentences: Your main debugging tool is called a trace.
At each numbered step, it records what Scout decided to do next.
It shows which tool Scout chose, and the exact input it sent.
And it shows what came back: a result, or an error.
Think of a flight recorder.
When something goes wrong, you replay exactly what happened instead of guessing.

slides.title: A healthy trace
slides.lead: agent.py prints one line for each tool call and one for its result. This run went well.

rows.out: uses the tracking number it just found
the arrival day for the reply

aside.label: Read it like a story
aside.text: Each step should follow from the one before. Where the story stops making sense, that's your bug.

sentences: Here is the trace of a healthy run.
Step one: Scout calls get order with Ana's order number.
The result comes back: shipped, with a tracking number.
Step two: Scout calls track parcel, using the tracking number it just found.
That result gives the arrival day, Thursday, which goes into the reply.
Read a trace like a story: each step should follow from the one before.
And when the reply and the trace disagree, trust the trace: it shows what Scout actually did.

slides.title: The debugging loop

center.label: Debug loop
center.sub: one failing case at a time

note.text: The first bad step matters most. Later mistakes often follow from it.

sentences: When a case fails, go round this loop.
Reproduce: run that one case on its own, with the trace on.
Read: walk the trace from the top and find the first step that's wrong.
Fix: change one thing, aimed at that step.
Re-run: first the failing case, then the whole test set, to be sure nothing else broke.
Focus on the first bad step, because later mistakes often follow from it.
One change per loop keeps cause and effect clear, just like building one piece at a time.

slides.title: Four bugs you will meet

cells: get_order with an email as order_id
An error, then a confident answer
The same call, again and again
Step limit plus a clearer error

note.text: Most agent bugs are one of these four. Name it, then fix it.

sentences: Most agent bugs fall into four families.
Wrong tool: Scout searches the policy when it should look up the order, usually because two descriptions overlap.
Wrong arguments: the right tool with the wrong input, like an email where an order number should be.
Ignored error: a tool fails, and Scout answers confidently anyway.
Looping: Scout calls the same tool again and again, hoping for a different result.
Once you can name the bug, the fix is usually clear.
Each family leaves its own fingerprint in the trace, so with practice you'll spot them at a glance.

slides.title: Reading a buggy trace

messages.label: Grace
messages.text: Hi, I ordered boots with grace@example.com. Can I return them?

messages.label: step 1
messages.text: get_order {"order_id": "grace@example.com"} → Error: No order with ID grace@example.com

messages.label: Scout
messages.text: Yes! You can return unused items within 30 days for a full refund.

messages.label: checker
messages.text: FAIL: no order was found, and the boots were delivered 62 days ago.

aside.label: Two bugs, one cause
aside.text: Step 1 has wrong arguments. The reply ignores the error. Fix step 1 first.

sentences: Now a trace from one of Scout's real failures.
Grace writes in with her email address, not an order number.
Step one: Scout calls get order, but puts her email in the order number field, and the tool returns an error.
Scout then answers anyway, cheerfully promising a return.
The checker fails it: her boots were delivered 62 days ago, well outside the window.
There are two bugs here, wrong arguments and an ignored error, but the first bad step is step one.
Fix that first, and the reply will have real data to work with.

slides.title: Catching a loop
slides.scenario: Elena asks where her climbing rope is. The carrier keeps timing out.

steps.text: track_parcel PP-90417 → Error: ParcelPath did not answer
The same call and the same timeout, four more times
MAX_STEPS ends the run with a polite apology
The error now says: don't retry, tell the customer tracking is down

result.text: The step limit kept the run cheap. The clearer error message fixed the cause.

sentences: The last bug is the loop, and it's the one that costs money.
Elena asks where her rope is, and the carrier times out.
Scout tries again, and again, with exactly the same call.
The step limit you added in Module 3 ends the run after six steps.
The real fix is a clearer error: the carrier isn't answering, so don't retry, and tell the customer.
The limit kept the run cheap, but only the better error message fixed the cause.

slides.title: Recap

points.text: A trace shows every step: the tool, its input, the result.
Reproduce, read, fix one thing, then re-run everything.
Find the first bad step; later ones often follow from it.
Name the bug: wrong tool, wrong arguments, ignored error, loop.

sentences: Let's recap.
A trace shows each step of a run: the tool, its input and its result.
To debug, reproduce the case, read the trace, fix one thing, and re-run everything.
Look for the first bad step, because later mistakes often follow from it.
And most bugs are one of four: wrong tool, wrong arguments, an ignored error, or a loop.
Next, we zoom out from one case to all of them, and measure Scout as a whole.

midQuiz.q: What does Scout's trace show for each step of a run?
options: Only the final reply to the customer
The tool Scout called, the input it sent, and the result or error
How many tokens each reply used
midQuiz.explain: A trace replays the run step by step: what Scout decided, which tool it called with what input, and what came back. That is what lets you find the bad step.

midQuiz.q: A failing case has three steps that look wrong. Where do you start?
options: The final reply, since that's what the customer saw
Whichever step looks easiest to fix
midQuiz.explain: Later steps work with what earlier steps produced. Fix the first bad step and the rest often fix themselves.
midQuiz.hint: Read the trace like a story, from the top.

endQuiz.q: The trace shows get_order called with order_id set to grace@example.com, then an error. Which bug is this?
endQuiz.explain: get_order was the right tool, but it got the wrong input: an email in the order ID field. The usual fix is in the tool's schema or description.
endQuiz.hint: Was the tool wrong, or what was passed to it?

endQuiz.q: Scout calls track_parcel six times in a row, timing out each time. What is the best fix?
options: Raise MAX_STEPS so Scout gets more tries
Make the error say not to retry and to tell the customer tracking is down
Delete track_parcel so it can't fail
endQuiz.explain: The step limit stops the damage, but the loop happens because the error gives Scout no better idea. A clear error message changes what it does next.
endQuiz.hint: What does Scout read right after each failed call?
